narrative_memory_primitives.content: When I think about my school years in Seoul, I often picture the walk near Dongduk Girls’ High School and the quiet hours I spent practicing songs instead of socializing. Even before debuting under LOEN Entertainment, music felt more familiar to me than classrooms or playgrounds.

Before signing with LOEN Entertainment, I remember moving between small audition rooms in Seoul, singing the same verses repeatedly. Many of those days blurred together, but they shaped the discipline I later carried into albums like Growing Up.

Standing backstage at KBS Music Bank after my debut with Lost and Found, I felt more nervous than excited. Seeing senior artists pass by reminded me how far I still had to go, even as my name began appearing on broadcast schedules.

When Good Day started climbing the charts, I spent long hours at broadcast stations like KBS and SBS, repeating the same high notes during rehearsals. The attention came quickly, and I leaned heavily on my staff at LOEN Entertainment to stay grounded.

While working on Palette, I often thought about how different my life felt compared to the Growing Up era. Collaborating with musicians and discussing lyrics with my team at EDAM Entertainment made me more aware of how much I had changed.

Late-night recording sessions became familiar during albums like Love Poem and Lilac. Sitting in Seoul studios, I often thought about how songs like Through the Night reflected quieter parts of myself that interviews never captured.

Filming My Mister alongside Lee Sun-kyun taught me how silence could carry emotion. On set, director Kim Won-seok often reminded me to trust stillness more than dialogue, which stayed with me long after filming ended.

Playing Jang Man-wol in Hotel del Luna required a different kind of preparation than my music work. Between costume fittings and late-night shoots in Seoul, I felt myself balancing fantasy storytelling with very real exhaustion.

Working on Broker with director Hirokazu Kore-eda felt very different from Korean dramas. Watching Song Kang-ho on set made me reflect on how film acting demands patience and restraint in ways television rarely does.

As people continued calling me the Nation’s Little Sister, I found myself moving carefully through public spaces in Seoul. Events like the Melon Music Awards reminded me how public perception can feel both supportive and distant at the same time.

Making donations through organizations during national disasters often felt quieter than performing on stage. Even while promoting albums like The Winning, I tried to separate public recognition from private intentions.

Looking back from projects like When Life Gives You Tangerines to early stages like Dream High, I can see how slowly my perspective shifted. Acting and music began to inform each other in ways I never expected at the beginning.
